checks.title: Sun and Earth direction from a lunar site
checks.result: Largest angular difference: Sun 0.0078 deg, Earth 0.0034 deg.
checks.detail: 6 site-and-period cases, 13220 table rows in total (Sun and Earth rows counted separately). Each row is the azimuth and elevation Horizons gives for a point on the Moon's surface; we recompute it with the in-browser engine and measure the angle between the two directions. The Sun is 0.53 deg wide, so a 0.01 deg difference is about 2% of its diameter.

checks.title: Terrain grids are read correctly
checks.reference: NASA Moon Trek elevation service (NASA Goddard study sites)
checks.result: Ground heights at five study sites agree within 16 m (largest) on heights of 775 m to 6386 m.
checks.detail: Ours / expected, metres: 1943 / 1945; 775 / 791; 1646 / 1638; 4794 / 4790; 6386 / 6402. The expected values came from a 30 m grid resampled to 200 m, so differences of this size are expected. Second check, run for the illumination comparison: our ground height at 21 polar sites against Moon Trek's 30 m LOLA elevation service (LRO_LOLA_DEM_SPole75_30mp_v04_SP), same coordinate mapping as the illumination comparison: median difference 1.5 m, largest 49.9 m (a steep crater-rim point where an 80 m and a 30 m grid sample a different slope). This also confirms the coordinate convention used to query the NASA maps.

checks.title: Skyline from synthetic terrain
checks.result: Flat sphere gives -0.087 deg at 2 m and -0.194 deg at 10 m (geometric dip -0.087 and -0.194 deg); a mountain due north peaks at azimuth 0 deg and one due east at 91 deg.
checks.detail: The flat case is a sphere of radius 1737.4 km with no relief, viewed from -85 deg latitude; every azimuth should sit at the dip -acos(R / (R + h)). The mountains are 2000 m high, 10 km away, 2 km wide, and their skyline reaches 11.3 deg (north) and 11.3 deg (east). The test passes if the peak lies within 1 deg of the true azimuth; the terrain grid used here has 500 m pixels, which at 10 km distance is 2.9 deg wide, so a peak 1 deg off is below the grid's own resolution.

checks.title: IM-1 Odysseus: Sun reaches the horizon
checks.reference: NASA JPL Horizons at 80.13 S, 1.44 E
checks.result: Engine: Sun centre 0.63 deg at 2024-03-03 00:00 UTC and -1.46 deg at 2024-03-04 00:00 UTC (Horizons: +0.6 and -1.5 deg). It crosses the smooth horizon at 2024-03-03 08:11 UTC.
checks.detail: Smooth sphere, no terrain, observer 2 m above ground; the smooth horizon at 2 m is -0.087 deg below level. The Horizons values are quoted to 0.1 deg. The check shows the engine places the Sun's setting at the right day and within about 1 hour of the Horizons elevation track; it does not test the terrain, which at the real landing point is Malapert A and its surroundings.

checks.title: Blue Ghost Mission 1: length of the lunar day
checks.reference: Firefly Aerospace mission report (about 346 hours of daylight operations)
checks.result: Engine: sunset 347.8 hours after landing at 2025-03-02 08:34 UTC, 18.56 N, 61.81 E; Firefly reported about 346 hours of daylight operations (difference 1.8 hours, 0.5%).
checks.detail: Smooth sphere with no terrain, observer 2 m above ground; "up" means at least half the Sun's disc above the horizon. The mission figure is rounded and counts operations, not the exact sunset time, so this is a plausibility check on the length of the lunar day, not a precision test.

checks.title: Average sunlight against NASA Goddard maps
checks.reference: NASA Goddard average Sun visibility maps (Mazarico et al. 2011 method, 2016 release), read from NASA Moon Trek
checks.result: Like-for-like, observer on the ground (0 m), 23 sites: correlation 0.98, median absolute difference 1.3 percentage points, mean difference (ours minus NASA) +2.0 points; largest difference Malapert Massif (NASA Goddard study site 23): ours 18.2%, NASA 4.6% (+13.6 points). At 2 m (shipped masks): correlation 0.97, median 3.8 points, mean +6.8 points, largest +26.0 points.
checks.detail: Quantity compared: share of time with any part of the Sun's disc above the skyline (NASA's definition), averaged over 18.6 years from 2020-01-01 every 2 hours (81523 samples; NASA uses hourly steps over a full nutation cycle but gives no calendar dates). NASA's maps are for the ground surface, so the 0 m skylines are the like-for-like comparison; they were computed directly from the LOLA 80 m and 240 m grids with the same code as the shipped masks, which are unchanged. At 2 m the largest difference is Connecting Ridge (NASA Goddard study site 1) — highest point within 8 km: ours 91.2%, NASA 65.2% (+26.0 points). At 10 m: correlation 0.89, median absolute difference 5.7 points, 5 sites more than 30 points apart. Rank correlation at 0 m 0.99. Crest points (5 derived highest-pixel sites): mean difference +7.5 points at 0 m against +15.6 at 2 m; other sites +0.5 at 0 m and +4.4 at 2 m. Observer height therefore explains about 52% of the crest difference at 2 m, and a mean difference of +7.5 points remains at crests. Remaining limitation: an 80 m grid cannot see relief smaller than about 80 m, so sunlight at ridge crests may be overestimated. Differences at 0 m range from -11.5 to +13.6 points over all sites; negative values occur where our rounded coordinates fall off the NASA crest. Mean disc fraction instead of any-part share at 0 m: correlation 0.98, median 0.9 points. Sites use the finest NASA map that covers them: 60 m (20 sites), 120 m (1), 240 m (2). Other caveats: NASA's maps are on a 60 m to 240 m grid and, per NASA's documentation, contain linear artefacts from the DEM; our site coordinates are rounded, so at ridge crests a 100 m shift changes the skyline by degrees. Status is 'note': ranking and median agreement are good, but the largest single-site difference is 14 points.

checks.title: Average illumination at Connecting Ridge against a published study
checks.reference: Barker et al. (2021), Planetary and Space Science 203, 105119, Table 2: Site 1 (Shackleton-de Gerlache connecting ridge), January 2024 to January 2026
checks.result: Ours, mean Sun disc fraction 2024-01-01 to 2026-01-01: crest point 88.0% at 2 m and 92.2% at 10 m; listed point 40.7% at 2 m and 79.0% at 10 m. Published best regions: about 67-71% at 1 m and about 83-89% at 5 m.
checks.detail: Plausibility check only. The published figures are first-percentile values over an ensemble of 100 elevation-model variants, for the best small regions on a 5 m grid at 1 m and 5 m above the ground; the digits were read from an image of the table. Ours are single points from an 80 m grid at 2 m and 10 m, hourly. Our crest point (the highest 80 m pixel within 8 km of the listed centre) is a favourable spot and gives 88.0% at 2 m, above the published 1 m range and at the top of the 5 m range, although 2 m is closer to 1 m than to 5 m; because the published values are first percentiles (pessimistic), a higher best estimate is not a contradiction, but it is not a match either. Our listed point sits off the crest and gives 40.7% at 2 m, well below the published best regions, as expected for a point that is not among the best. The result is consistent with the published picture (a few tens of percent at 1 m rising by about 15-20 points at 5 m) but cannot confirm our numbers to better than about 20 percentage points.

checks.title: Eclipses: Earth crossing the Sun, against NASA's eclipse table
checks.reference: NASA lunar eclipse table 2021-2030 (F. Espenak, eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov): ten lunar eclipses in 2027-2030
checks.result: Engine, whole near side of the Moon, 2027-2030: 10 of NASA's 10 eclipses found, each within 1 minute of NASA's time of greatest eclipse; 0 extra.
checks.detail: Earth's disc includes a 75 km opaque layer of atmosphere (Danjon's method, used by NASA's eclipse predictions). An eclipse counts if Earth covers part of the Sun anywhere on the Moon's near side, as the table does; at a single site a shallow eclipse may not be seen at all. NASA's times are Terrestrial Dynamical Time, about a minute ahead of UTC.

checks.title: Deep Space Network: Moon elevation at Goldstone, Canberra and Madrid
checks.reference: NASA JPL Horizons, Moon seen from the 70 m antennas (positions from DSN handbook 810-005, module 301 Rev. N, Table 5), hourly for a week, no refraction
checks.result: Largest elevation difference: Goldstone 0.0007 deg, Canberra 0.0008 deg, Madrid 0.0008 deg.
checks.detail: Contact needs Earth in view from the lander and the Moon at least 6 degrees up at a complex (the handbook gives the mechanical limit as approximately six degrees). Terrain masks at the complexes, refraction and antenna scheduling are not modelled.

checks.title: Sunlit and Earth-in-view, date by date, at Malapert Massif
checks.reference: ACT's Artemis III Geotechnical cubes in LROC QuickMap: Malapert Massif, 2 m pixels, every 6 h, December 2025, lit by the Sun's centre
checks.result: Ground level, 25,425 point-and-time cases: Sun verdict agrees in 95.2%, Earth in 97.4%.
checks.detail: Where the Sun verdicts differ, it is lit only in ours in 425 cases and only in theirs in 792. Their terrain is finer (NASA Goddard 5 m site maps and LROC NAC elevation models); ours is LDEM_85S_10M, LDEM_80S_20M, LDEM_60S_240M.

checks.result: Ours, mean Sun disc fraction at the crest point: 58.0% at 1 m, 70.6% at 2 m, 84.2% at 5 m, 89.3% at 10 m.
checks.detail: Terrain: LDEM_85S_10M, LDEM_80S_20M, LDEM_60S_240M. The published figures are for the best area of the site; ours are one point, so this is a plausibility check.
